findings.title: Team permission check uses && instead of ||, rejecting team admins
findings.body: The authorization check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamAdmin already matches memberships with role ADMIN or OWNER, so AND-ing it with isTeamOwner makes the whole expression equivalent to "user is team owner". Team admins — whom the variable name and the feature intend to allow — will always fail this check and hit the FORBIDDEN branch, so they cannot add guests to team bookings. The `&&` should be `||`.

findings.title: Any attendee can add guests, triggering organizer-branded emails to arbitrary addresses
findings.body: The handler authorizes the request when `isAttendee` is true — any person whose email happens to be on the booking can call viewer.bookings.addGuests with arbitrary addresses. Each call sends an AttendeeScheduledEmail "from" the organizer (replyTo the organizer) to the new addresses plus a notification to every existing attendee. A malicious attendee can therefore spam third parties using the organizer's identity and the booking's legitimacy, with no consent from the organizer and no cap on guests per call. If attendee-initiated guest additions are intentional, this needs rate limiting and sending from the attendee's identity; otherwise the endpoint should be restricted to the organizer and team admins/owners.

findings.title: Calendar update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's, after attendees are already written
findings.body: `eventManager` is built from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person making the request — but the calendar event being updated lives on the organizer's calendar (booking.user, which is already fetched with credentials in the booking query but never used). When a team owner/admin or an attendee adds guests, EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees searches the requester's credentials for one matching booking.references, which is either missing (throws) or belongs to the wrong user. Because prisma.booking.update has already created the Attendee rows before this call and the call is not wrapped in error handling, the mutation then returns an error even though the guests were persisted: the user sees "unable to add guests", the organizer's calendar event is never updated with the new attendees, and retrying fails with "emails_must_be_unique_valid" because the attendees already exist. Use the organizer's credentials and make the flow failure-safe (e.g., update the calendar before committing, or handle errors so the user is not told the operation failed when it half-succeeded).

findings.title: No check on booking status or date before adding guests
findings.body: After loading the booking, the handler never checks booking.status or the booking time, so guests can be added to CANCELLED, REJECTED, PENDING or past bookings. This is reachable from the UI for past confirmed bookings (BookingListItem renders the Edit → "Additional guests" action for `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed`) and via direct API calls for cancelled/rejected ones. Adding a guest to a cancelled booking emails them an AttendeeScheduledEmail with a CONFIRMED ics for an event that no longer exists and permanently attaches attendees to a dead booking. Reject non-ACCEPTED and past bookings before creating attendees.

findings.title: Guest dedupe and blacklist checks are case-sensitive
findings.body: uniqueGuests filters with `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is not, so `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entirely. Likewise `Existing@Email.com` is not recognized as matching an existing attendee `existing@email.com`, so a duplicate Attendee row is created (the client-side uniqueness refine has the same case-sensitivity problem). Normalize case (and trim whitespace) on the input before comparing.

findings.title: sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type settings that disable standard emails
findings.body: Every other send* function in this file accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails when eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail is set (event types can disable standard emails, e.g. for custom workflows/platform customers). sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata parameter and addGuests.handler doesn't pass one, so organizers and attendees of event types with standard emails disabled will still receive "Guests Added" and booking-confirmation emails whenever a guest is added, breaking that contract. Thread eventTypeMetadata through and honor the disable flags.

findings.title: Adding guests to seated events bypasses seat reservation logic
findings.body: For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be created together with a BookingSeat record (the handleSeats flow) so that seat availability is counted and the attendee can later cancel/reschedule their seat. This handler blindly creates plain Attendee rows via createMany for any event type, so for seated events the new guests consume no seat — the slot can be overbooked through the normal booking flow afterwards — and the guests have no seat reference for seat-based operations. The handler should either reject seated event types or route through the seat-booking logic.

findings.title: New guests are stored with the organizer's timeZone and locale
findings.body: guestsFullDetails sets `timeZone: organizer.timeZone` and `locale: organizer.locale` for every added guest. The AttendeeScheduledEmail sent to those guests renders the meeting time in the attendee's stored timezone — which is actually the organizer's — so guests in other timezones see a wrong local time presented as theirs, and the attendee record permanently carries the wrong timezone/locale (affecting reminders and future emails too). Consider storing a neutral value or making clear whose timezone is displayed.

findings.title: No limit on number of guests per request
findings.body: `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no .max(), and each call sends an email to every existing attendee plus every new guest, and performs a calendar update. A single request can add hundreds of guests, fanning out hundreds of emails and a large calendar payload — an abuse and performance footgun even for a legitimate organizer. Add a sane .max() on the array and consider a per-booking total guest limit.

findings.title: No tests for the new addGuests mutation
findings.body: The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that performs a non-trivial permission matrix (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), dedupes against existing attendees and a blacklist, writes Attendee rows, updates calendars and sends emails, but adds no unit or integration tests. The permission matrix, duplicate/blacklist filtering, seated-event handling and cancelled-booking behavior are exactly where this implementation has defects; tests covering those cases should be added before merging.
